narrative.summary: Australia has no AI-specific Act. Its National AI Plan (December 2025) relies on existing laws, a new Australian AI Safety Institute and voluntary guidance rather than the mandatory guardrails for high-risk AI proposed in 2024, which were not taken forward. AI-relevant Commonwealth law includes the Privacy Act, which from 10 December 2026 requires privacy policies to disclose substantially automated decisions, the 2024 offences for deepfake sexual material, the generative-AI expectations in the Basic Online Safety Expectations, and provisions allowing decisions by computer program in social security, migration, citizenship and NDIS law. Government use of AI is governed by the Digital Transformation Agency's mandatory policy for responsible use of AI (version 2.0 from December 2025), with its AI technical standard, impact assessment tool and transparency statements, and by the national framework for the assurance of AI in government agreed with the states in 2024; the National AI Centre's Guidance for AI Adoption (2025) replaced the Voluntary AI Safety Standard. Regulators add guidance and enforcement: the privacy regulator's AI guidance and facial recognition determinations, eSafety's online safety standard covering generative AI, ASIC's review of AI governance in financial services, APRA's 2026 letter on AI and the TGA's review of AI in medical device software. The Federal Court and the Federal Circuit and Family Court issued rules on court users' use of AI in 2026, and a 2025 security direction requires Commonwealth entities to remove DeepSeek products. New South Wales has the most developed state regime, with a mandatory AI Operational Policy and AI Assessment Framework; Victoria, Queensland and Western Australia (whose new privacy law adds automated-decision duties from July 2026) have their own policies, and the City of Adelaide has an AI policy.

instruments.official_title: Guidance on privacy and the use of commercially available AI products
instruments.english_title: Guidance on privacy and the use of commercially available AI products
instruments.issuing_authority: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
instruments.publisher_name: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner
instruments.current_status: Published by the OAIC on 21 October 2024; the page shows an update on 17 January 2025. Guidance on how the Privacy Act 1988 and the Australian Privacy Principles apply; it does not create new obligations. Companion to the OAIC guidance on developing and training generative AI models.
instruments.summary: OAIC guidance for organisations deploying commercially available or freely available AI products (chatbots, content generators, productivity assistants) that handle personal information. It explains how APPs 1, 3, 5, 6 and 10 apply to AI inputs and outputs, treating AI-generated or inferred information (including hallucinations and deepfakes) about an identifiable person as personal information, and calls for due diligence, privacy impact assessments and transparent privacy policies. As best practice it recommends that organisations do not enter personal, and especially sensitive, information into publicly available generative AI tools; it comes with a quick reference guide and two checklists.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: The privacy regulator's main guidance on deploying AI products under the Privacy Act.

instruments.official_title: Privacy Act 1988
instruments.english_title: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) (No. 119, 1988)
instruments.issuing_authority: Parliament of Australia
instruments.current_status: Act No. 119, 1988, assented to 14 December 1988 and commenced 1 January 1989 (endnotes of the compilation). Latest compilation read: Compilation No. 104, compilation date 4 June 2026 (includes amendments up to Act No. 75, 2025). Uncommenced amendments listed on the Register: Schedule 1 items 87-88 of the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 (automated-decision transparency in APP privacy policies, new APP 1.7-1.9) commence on 10 December 2026; Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Act 2026 amendments from 1 January 2027. The statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy (Schedule 2, inserted by the 2024 amending Act) has been in force since 10 June 2025. A further reform package (exposure draft Privacy Amendment (Personal Data Protection) Bill 2026) was released for consultation on 31 August 2026 and is not law. Until 10 December 2026 the Act contains no provision specific to AI or automated decisions; it is recorded as the general privacy law governing personal information used to train and deploy AI.
instruments.summary: Australia's general information-privacy law. It binds Australian Government agencies and private-sector organisations with annual turnover above $3 million (plus certain smaller businesses such as health service providers) through the 13 Australian Privacy Principles covering open and transparent management, collection, use and disclosure, cross-border disclosure, data quality, security, access and correction of personal information, with enforcement by the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) including civil penalties and the notifiable data breaches scheme. Schedule 2 (from 10 June 2025) gives individuals a statutory cause of action in tort for serious invasions of privacy, and from 10 December 2026 APP 1.7-1.9 require privacy policies to disclose the use of computer programs to make, or substantially assist, decisions that significantly affect individuals' rights or interests.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: General privacy law governing personal information used to develop, train and deploy AI; from 10 December 2026 contains an express transparency duty for automated decisions (APP 1.7-1.9).

instruments.official_title: Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024
instruments.english_title: Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024 (No. 128, 2024)
instruments.issuing_authority: Parliament of Australia
instruments.current_status: Act No. 128, 2024, assented to 10 December 2024 (bill introduced 12 September 2024, finally passed both Houses 29 November 2024). Commencement (s 2): ss 1-4 on assent (10 December 2024); Schedule 1 Parts 1-14 (including the Children's Online Privacy Code mandate, new penalties and OAIC powers) on 11 December 2024; Schedule 3 (doxxing offences in the Criminal Code) on 11 December 2024; Schedule 2 (statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy) on 10 June 2025 (default 6-month commencement); Schedule 1 Part 15 (automated decisions and privacy policies) on 10 December 2026, i.e. not yet in force at the verification date. The OAIC must develop and register the Children's Online Privacy Code within 24 months of assent (by 10 December 2026; the code itself is recorded under the OAIC's work). The amendments are incorporated in the Privacy Act 1988 compilation.
instruments.summary: First tranche of Privacy Act reforms. It amends the Privacy Act 1988 to require the Information Commissioner to develop a Children's Online Privacy Code binding social media, relevant electronic and designated internet services likely to be accessed by children, adds tiered civil penalties, infringement notices and new OAIC inquiry and determination powers, allows eligible data-breach and emergency information sharing, and clarifies security obligations and overseas disclosures. Schedule 1 Part 15 inserts APP 1.7-1.9, under which an APP entity that arranges for a computer program to make, or do a thing substantially and directly related to making, a decision that could reasonably be expected to significantly affect an individual's rights or interests using their personal information must state in its privacy policy the kinds of personal information used and the kinds of decisions made solely or substantially by computer programs (from 10 December 2026); Schedule 2 creates a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy and Schedule 3 creates Criminal Code doxxing offences.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Introduces Australia's first statutory transparency obligation for automated decision-making using personal information (APP 1.7-1.9, from 10 December 2026) and the Children's Online Privacy Code mandate.

instruments.official_title: Criminal Code Amendment (Deepfake Sexual Material) Act 2024
instruments.english_title: Criminal Code Amendment (Deepfake Sexual Material) Act 2024 (No. 78, 2024)
instruments.issuing_authority: Parliament of Australia
instruments.current_status: Act No. 78, 2024, assented to 2 September 2024; the whole Act commenced the day after assent, 3 September 2024 (s 2). Bill introduced 5 June 2024, finally passed both Houses 21 August 2024 (aph.gov.au bill page r7205). The amendments are incorporated in the Criminal Code Act 1995 compilation.
instruments.summary: Replaces the Criminal Code offence in s 474.17A with an offence of using a carriage service to transmit sexual material depicting an adult without their consent (or being reckless as to consent), punishable by 6 years' imprisonment, and makes it irrelevant whether the material is unaltered or has been created or altered using technology; the legislative note expressly covers images, video or audio edited or entirely created with digital technology including artificial intelligence ('deepfakes'). New s 474.17AA adds aggravated offences carrying 7 years' imprisonment, including where the offender was responsible for creating or altering the material, and where 3 or more civil penalty orders under the Online Safety Act have previously been made against the person.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Criminalises non-consensual sharing of sexual deepfakes, including AI-generated material, with an aggravated offence for creating it.

instruments.summary: The Act that administers Australia's social security law. It is the longest-standing Commonwealth authorisation of automated decision-making, cited by the Attorney-General's Department as the model for later provisions and relevant to the Robodebt scheme's administration.

instruments.issuing_authority: Attorney-General's Department
instruments.current_status: Exposure draft and consultation paper released for public consultation by the Attorney-General's Department; consultation opened 31 August 2026 and closed 18 September 2026 (AGD consultation hub). instruments.summary: Second tranche of Privacy Act reform: an exposure draft Bill of about 40 proposals (25 Privacy Act Review proposals uplifting protections, 5 clarifying and simplifying obligations, 4 further simplification measures and 7 OAIC efficiency measures). It would modernise core definitions (personal information, sensitive information, de-identified, collects, consent), replace collection, use and disclosure rules with a single 'fair and reasonable' test, strengthen consent, notification, direct-marketing, data security, minimisation and breach-response requirements, create a right to request erasure from large digital platforms and reduce obligations for processors; the consultation paper notes the amended meaning of 'collects' covers personal information generated or derived through data analysis or artificial intelligence, and frames the reforms as addressing risks from AI and wearable devices.
instruments.ai_governance_relevance: Proposed overhaul of the general privacy law, expressly treating AI-inferred personal information as collected information.

instruments.publisher_name: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner

instruments.summary: OAIC guidance for developers who design, build, train, adapt or combine generative AI models or systems, including fine-tuning, on how the Privacy Act and APPs 1, 3, 5, 6 and 10 apply to training data. It also sets expectations on accuracy (high-quality datasets, testing, disclaimers), privacy by design and transparency.

instruments.publisher_name: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner

Under s 52(1A) Clearview was declared to stop collecting scraped and probe images and vectors from individuals in Australia and to destroy those already collected within 90 days.

instruments.current_status: Letter to all APRA-regulated entities published 30 April 2026. APRA states its prudential framework is technology-agnostic and that it is finalising a forward plan for supervising AI risks; the letter does not create new prudential standards.
instruments.summary: Letter to all APRA-regulated banks, insurers and superannuation trustees setting out findings of a late-2025 targeted review of large entities, which found governance, risk management, assurance and operational resilience lagging AI adoption. Information obtained under court orders, subpoena or subject to suppression must not be entered into a generative AI tool unless it stays in a closed environment, is not used for training and is used only for that proceeding.

instruments.summary: TGA guidance on when digital (AI or ambient) scribes are regulated as medical devices under the Therapeutic Goods Act 1989. Scribes that only record, transcribe or summarise clinical conversations are not medical devices, while those that suggest diagnoses or treatments, triage patients or generate clinical conclusions are, and must be included in the ARTG. Intended purpose is judged from labelling, marketing and design, general disclaimers are not accepted, and developers must reassess regulatory status when they add features.

coverage_audit.technical_note:
Method note (original): Deep review completed on 11 October 2026, covering Commonwealth laws, bills and legislative instruments, federal departments and agencies, federal regulators, all six states and two territories, and the cities of Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Adelaide, Perth, Gold Coast, Parramatta and Hobart. Many official websites could not be read automatically, including the Australian Cyber Security Centre, the eSafety Commissioner, the ACCC, the Australian Human Rights Commission and most South Australian, Tasmanian, ACT and Northern Territory government sites; records from those sites are marked as located but not fully read, or held as pending. Bills before Parliament are listed as pending rather than as instruments. Pending: eSafety's online safety codes covering AI companion chatbots, the ACCC's digital platform reports on AI, the Human Rights Commission's 2021 report on human rights and technology, the TGA's guidance on digital scribes, the ACT and South Australian AI policies, and the founding documents of the Australian AI Safety Institute.

Coverage note (original): Technical review notes: Backfill run 2026-10-11 in five parts (A1 federal law and bills; A2 federal government; A3 federal regulators; A4 states and territories; A5 cities). No usage-limit interruption occurred; every record was built from official texts read in this run and the six earlier records were re-checked and fixed (domain-named publishers and organisations replaced). sandbox: no AI regulatory sandbox found (ASIC, APRA, DISR and state sites searched). index-readiness: no government-published AI readiness index or maturity assessment found. Access: cyber.gov.au and asd.gov.au (bot protection), dta.gov.au blog and media pages, esafety.gov.au (reset/503), accc.gov.au and humanrights.gov.au (403), tga.gov.au and health.gov.au (timeouts), parlinfo.aph.gov.au (403), NSW legislation and Parliament, IPC NSW, OIC Queensland, and most SA, Tasmanian, ACT and NT government hosts (403). Several industry.gov.au, digital.gov.au and finance.gov.au pages timing out on direct requests were read through a text-rendering fetch of the official URL (r.jina.ai), recorded in each source's check_method. TGA documents were read on the TGA consultation hub (consultations.tga.gov.au). DISR consultation PDFs are served from the consult.industry.gov.au platform's storage host, linked from the DISR consultation page (source_url is the DISR page). OAIC determinations cite the determination itself (PROTOCOL §1): Clearview [2021] AICmr 54 from the determination PDF on oaic.gov.au; Bunnings [2024] AICmr 230 and Kmart [2025] AICmr 155 from the OAIC privacy determinations register (full texts are published on AustLII, which returned 403; the OAIC-hosted Kmart PDF returned 404). 28 records are primary_source_located, including 9 state and territory records built from search-engine copies of official texts; world events whose dates came only from those copies (NSW Act No 57 of 2025 assent and commencement, SA depictions Act assent, Tasmanian guidance approval, NT AI Assurance Framework release) were not logged. The Basic Online Safety Expectations were found by A1 and A3 and are recorded once. The Privacy Act APP 1.7-1.9 automated-decision transparency commences 10 Dec 2026 and is not logged as a world event until it commences. The eSafety designated internet services standard effective date is left empty pending confirmation from eSafety's register. Brisbane, Perth, Gold Coast and Parramatta: no AI instrument found on official council sources. Second-method retry (BACKFILL step 4) on 2026-10-11: all 28 located-only records were retried with WebFetch and curl. IPP 10 under SL 2026/128 is confirmed in the consolidation's commencement table).
